abstract: This lecture, delivered by Dr. Calvert, covers the clinical evaluation and management of six common adnexal mass presentations. Through case-based teaching, the speaker emphasizes the importance of taking a thorough sexual and menstrual history, linking symptoms such as dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and pelvic fullness to specific diagnoses like endometriosis, hemorrhagic ovarian cyst, hydrosalpinx, and tubo-ovarian abscess. Ultrasound interpretation is highlighted, with particular attention to the 'ground glass' appearance of endometriomas. The lecture also reinforces the role of the pelvic exam, fertility counseling, and clinical reasoning to narrow the differential before imaging.
key_points: Assess sexual history (age at first intercourse, lifetime partners) to identify risk for STDs and PID.
Sudden severe pelvic pain that migrates from left to right suggests intraperitoneal fluid from a ruptured hemorrhagic cyst.
Endometrioma appears on ultrasound as a cystic ovarian structure with homogeneous 'ground glass' internal echoes.
Dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and infertility together strongly suggest endometriosis with possible endometrioma.
Cervical purulent discharge indicates gonorrhea or chlamydia infection, which can ascend to cause adnexal abscess.
Hydrosalpinx is a dilated, fluid-filled fallopian tube often resulting from prior PID and appears hypoechoic on ultrasound.
Regular menstrual periods imply ovulation; timing intercourse daily from day 5-15 may decrease sperm count and fertility.
Pelvic exam should include bimanual palpation if the examiner is skilled; limited uterine mobility suggests adhesions from prior infection or endometriosis.
Asymptomatic patients with history of STDs still warrant a pelvic exam because many infections (e.g., chlamydia) are asymptomatic.
Hemorrhagic ovarian cysts are common; most can be managed observationally if the patient is stable and pain controlled.
Complex ovarian cysts with septations and solid components should be considered ovarian cancer until proven otherwise.
Most women with ovarian cancer are symptomatic at the time of diagnosis.
